item.title: Reciprocity
item.description:
This is a follow-up to a previous post, In My Misanthropy Era.


In 2025, after getting my intellectual rocks off largely at hardcore rationality meetups for the entirety of the 2020s, I went to a casual philosophy meetup and it ~turned me evil. I wrote a post about this experience, because I thought it was interesting how a thoughtfully facilitated, pleasantly intellectual night out for most well-adjusted people was somehow my own personal hell. Also, that was objectively kind of a funny thing to have happened to me.

I was pleased with the final essay, so I crossposted it to LessWrong on a whim, where it promptly racked up a hundred comments and a bunch of discourse.

The comments were great! They were like dowsing rods, if dowsing rods were real and pointed you towards only incorrect conclusions. Having a dozen sincere, thoughtfully premised hypotheses for how I fucked up, all subtly wrong, was really useful for triangulating how I actually fucked up. I am genuinely grateful to all of the commenters, especially the ones who took time to write paragraphs and engage in extended back-and-forths with me. I am also grateful for Cunningham's law.

#MyRainforestPatch

In In My Misanthropy Era, I claim:

I was also very aware how much of a delicate baby I am when it comes to [epistemic/conversational norms] that I find tolerable. I am like one of those tree frog species that lives exclusively within a backyard-sized patch in the amazon rainforest, and I will be killed by like, the subtle change in microbiota if I step a toe outside it.

What the analogy leaves out is that I didn't end up in this patch by sheer chance! Actually, I worked really hard to make my home in that specific patch of rainforest — to build social circles in such a way that I am not smarter than most of the other people inside them. I did this because one of my favourite things is being intellectually outclassed. Intelligence is good, and when talking to smarter people, I get more book recommendations, more nuanced takes, more conversations that are deeper and more expansive.1

At the same time, I don't want to be around smarter people and feel slavish gratitude that they give me the time of day out of, like, noblesse oblige, or like I'm drawing down some kind of credit. I want to make it worth their while to hang out with me. I want to do little enlightened exchanges that leave everyone better off.

And the wonderful thing about not being the smartest person in the room is that it provides so much optionality in how I do that. I host silly events and go on snack runs and write dumb blog posts about, like, the footwear at Lighthaven without feeling a dereliction of duty, like I'm somehow defecting from this comparative advantage thing.

Ungated Discussion Groups Are Uniquely Bad Patches for Jenns, It's True

I like being prosocial! I enjoy treating fellow humans with dignity, finding viable reciprocal trades, and then being generous when trading. But the viability of trade depends on there being something worth having on both sides. In an environment where the only thing anyone could do was discuss very introductory philosophical questions, I wasn’t enthusiastic about any of the few trades on offer.

A few things contributed to this poor dynamic. First, the event ran on rails, which meant that a broad swathe of trades was off the table. For example, I couldn't get someone to go on a tangent with me about their amazing vintage coat without feeling like I was doing something wrong.

Second, the event was structured to punish intelligence, which also barred certain trades (e.g. what were to me more exciting and generative forms of disagreement). This is a legitimate trade-off that serves important goals. Certainly it makes sense to do so in philosophy groups which aim for maximal accessibility across a broad spectrum of people.

What do I mean when I say that it punishes intelligence? I mean that people who are smarter than others must work to either hide or disavow it, in service of keeping the atmosphere inclusive towards beginners. Sure, you can put additional care into being particularly graceful and socially adept if you want to display a little more intelligence, but having to do this extra work is precisely what I'm gesturing at. This is a real midwit's trap: if you're sufficiently intelligent, this additional cost is trivial to pay. But yours truly is not enough stdevs away from the mean for it to not pinch!

So I was penned in, quite awkwardly. I wanted to be a good participant, but there were not that many ways left to do that. Actually, there was only one thing remaining that I felt like I could offer, which was to be a good conversational partner. One that actively listens, asks thoughtful questions, and lets others speak and feel seen.

But this was a terrible trade for me, because what I got in exchange were increasingly terrible takes that I hated, by people who were increasingly convinced that I liked them and valued their opinions. I challenge anyone to not turn into the joker in such circumstances.2

In this framing, the contempt I felt emerged because I'd been placed in a position where the only prosocial option was a form of charity I don't find rewarding, with people I don't identify with, in exchange for nothing I value. The contempt was a signal that I needed to leave, and if I was wiser, I would have listened.

Some commenters note that the philosophy meetup is a worse place for me than a generic townie bar, and that's true. There are more kinds of trade that I can do at a bar, which means there's a higher chance that I can find one that is satisfactory. But I don't really anticipate having a particularly good time at the bar, either. I can perform the dutiful song and dance, talk to people and engage with them as full humans. But what I value — what feels scarce, what I actually spend effort and resources chasing — are environments that make me feel intellectually mediocre.

And since intelligence is broadly uncorrelated or positively correlated with other things I value from other humans (stories, skills, outrageousness, observations, humour, generosity, connection, cool outfits for me to appreciate, mouths that I can kiss, other things too I'm sure), those things are not exactly in short supply in my rainforest patch, so there's not really a good reason for me to leave and go to a bar instead.3

What Fixes Me

Here's a day trip I went on recently. Zvi had put out a monthly roundup, which mentioned that he and Tyler Cowen and Scott Sumner all agreed that Resurrection is a really good movie.4

So I pulled up the showtimes, and to my dismay, the last screening in the entirety of southern Ontario was that very evening, in an indie theatre in Toronto, which was a two hour train ride away. I texted J, a local rat who is frequently down for last-minute hangouts, and she agreed to meet me at the station.

Because the train does not come that often, I ended up arriving three hours before the show, and we had some time to wander around the area.

We came across the newly opened National Portrait Gallery of Canada of Bloorcourt, a cheeky little gallery, and popped in. Amongst other good works was this absolutely stunning photograph that kept rewarding me with more and more lovely detail the more I looked at it: the Canadiana, the composition, the light and shadows, the bright and lovely pops of buttercup yellow.5

We chatted a bit with the curators, who regaled us with the sorry history of the attempt to get an official Canadian portrait gallery For Real, an endeavour that was killed by the Harper administration. I complimented them on the curation of their own gallery, and meant it.

Afterwards, with more time to kill, we wandered into a wine bar because it had a pretty blue door, even though neither of us were big wine drinkers.

We arrived at a slow time, so the sommelier treated us to an impromptu wine tasting of two whites and two reds, all delicious. I got to ask many dumb questions ("are orange wines made with oranges?") and learned about how the wine industry changed over the last two decades from several different factors — climate change, increased demand from Asia and South America, natural wine blowing up.

In the end, to celebrate our Chinese heritage, we split a bottle of icewine. IYKYK. It was better chilled, so the sommelier popped it into the fridge for us while we wandered out to Mac's Pizza for an early dinner before returning for it.

Then at last we went into the theatre and saw Resurrection, which was two hours of one beautiful shot after another. It was also, frankly, quite challenging to piece together what was happening in the film, and I'm pretty sure it wasn't just because we were wine drunk for the first hour. After, we spent our subway ride to Union Station trying to figure out the plot of what we'd just watched, and did not get much closer to understanding by the end of it.

Then I went home, which took me until one in the morning because intercity transit SUCKS, but I didn't regret a single moment of the day, nor a single conversation. I left my rainforest patch, and of course it chafed a little, but I was glad to have done it. I came home richer.




  1. Sadly, it also subjects me to more incredibly painful drive-by puns in conversation, but I suppose no rainforest patch is perfect.↩

  2. I kind of had a sense of "there but for the grace of god" wrt not being in the mom's position in this post. Somehow the mom did not turn into the Joker, which I suppose is existence proof that it can be done by the sufficiently virtuous.↩

  3. I mean I guess there are not that many hot single lesbians inside it. But 1) that's, tragically, a worldwide shortage and 2) we might still be doing better than most patches due to the relative abundance of catgirls?↩

  4. ...Yes, this happened like nine months ago, before I moved to Toronto. I sware I've done more patch outings since then; it's just that this blog post has been stuck in the drafts for eight months. You know how it is :')↩

  5. I didn't notice the yellow until J pointed it out. Going to look at art with friends is very good↩

during a recent commute i was stopped at a red light when a bohemianly dressed, silver-haired asian woman crossed the street in front of me, talking to her companion in perfect, unaccented english.

how the times change, and assumptions dissolve with it! i hope it does not take until my own hair is silver all over, for me to stop being surprised by it.

item.title: Is [insert community] toxic?
item.description:
For any subculture or community - say, rationality, or raving, or crossfit, or social justice advocacy, or open source software, there are people who were once very devout members, but are now jaded haters. I think what's happening is that originally the community was so good for them that it hurt for them to consider that any part of it could be bad or toxic or harmful. Then, they were themselves hurt by one of the toxic elements, and there was some sort of sign flip, and suddenly it hurt for them to consider that there was anything good at all in the thing that did them harm.1

The reality is that any scene, being made up of flawed humans and flawed incentive structures, will have both good elements and toxic ones. The best communities will have relatively little toxicity while the worst communities will have a lot, but there's no scene where you can totally escape the risk of harm.

The best one can do is to be aware of this, so you can protect yourself when you partake in this thing that is nourishing to you.

If you care about the scene enough to become a custodian of it, this will also enable you to actually help address and minimize the presence of the toxic elements. You will need to acknowledge that they exist before you can do that. You will need to be able to say, "yes, this community has a tendency to hurt people in these ways, but it is still valuable and worth preserving, so let's put in the work to reduce the harm."

There are scenes that are not worth preserving. (Many would make that claim about some of mine.) But what I notice is that the scenes that have enough social sophistication and care to self-correct are the ones that are the healthiest.





  1. Notably, people who drift out of a scene gradually generally don't become haters.↩

item.title: Parallels
item.description:
There is nothing for you where you grow up. Most of the people who are like you you know only online handles of, and you'll have to go to a big city to find others like you in person. If you can make it out, you hear the biggest and most glamorous contingent is out in the bay area.

==

You were different from others, in a way that made it so that you were unpleasant to be around. Your peers did not take pains to hide this from you. You learn, slowly and carefully over your second decade of existence, how much it hurts to hide who you are, and how much it hurts others around you when you do not.

You build a little shell around yourself. You find ways to be otherwise likeable, valuable. You take on a certain apologism for the way you are.

The first time you meet more of your kind in person, it is in a quiet bar in a new city where you otherwise know no one. How queer the sensation, to have looked around at every strange new face, and felt at home.

They didn't just tolerate you; they liked you, liked your perspectives, thought about the world in the same way.

You had not even dreamt that such a thing could happen. The most you'd ever wished for, back then, was a friend or two who would take you as you are, even if they didn't quite understand.

==

You didn't choose to be this way. It would be easier, in many ways, if you weren't. But now that you've found people who are like you, you wouldn't give it up for the world.

==

The idea that it's a cult kind of makes you laugh. You're not building this for anyone except the people who are already one of you, or feel a longing to be. You're building this for the ghost of your eighteen year old self, alone and made awkward by the loneliness.

The thought of outsiders coming into your spaces brings you no joy at all. Haven't they taken enough from you? Why can't they all just fuck off and leave you alone? You leave the door open, though, because it's the only way to guarantee that the people who need to find you, will.

==

Grouphouses at 35. No timeline for kids, no timeline for retirement. When you join this community you stop having a traditional future.

==

Wiser members of your community tell you that despite the chasm of understanding, the mutual mislike, you need to make an effort to make yourself palatable to the wider world. There are larger things at stake.

So you self-police, try to clean up your image. Exhort others to do the same.

The people you're most embarrassed by are the ones with nowhere else to go.

==

"I just don't see why they have to make it their whole personality."

==

For the local festival last year you took them out to Hanlan's Point. You have to warn people not to go into the bushes south of the beach without knowing what they're getting in for, because it's an active cruise site even in the middle of the day.

There's an idle hope that the location helps the not insignificant queer and trans contingent feel a little better about swimming in public, but the reason you do it is because you feel better there. One more group of weirdos, on this beach that was claimed by people like you a century ago. A little continuity.

==

Trying to clock each other, in the wild.

==

You hear "you're one of the good ones," often, with barely any irony. What they mean is that you can pass.

One friend introduces you to his new girlfriend as a member of the community, and then immediately goes about describing them in the worst possible light. What makes him think it's okay to talk to you like that? Why do you let him talk to you like that, what do you think you win by refusing to flinch?

Another friend throws up her hands after her rant about your kind leaves you visibly upset. You know I like you, she says, and I like all your friends. It's true; she's in the discords, she's at the festivals. She's even helped you run them. She's proven herself an ally, so why is it that she isn't allowed to speak her truth without you blowing up at her?

You try to give everyone the benefit of the doubt. Perhaps they don't know how to relate to you. Perhaps they don't know how to relate to the part of themselves that are too like you. Perhaps it's your own fault, somehow.

==

Without the community, you would have strangled this part of yourself to death, in order to survive and to fit in with the rest of the world.

If you were born a hundred years ago, you would have found yourself a husband and a normal life. Or perhaps you would have become a very weird nun. Or killed yourself. Not known that life can be this sweet and wonderful. That you can have this form of relief. That you were numb in the first place.

==

Modify your body, transcend the flesh. Take the strange drugs that are available on the party circuit.

==

The community, its cultures and conventions, the meaning, the goodness, the joy, the grief, the way it makes you feel like you're close to dying, the way it makes you feel immortal — it separates you from a normal life, it separates you from your family.

You can't even come out to them. What you are is illegible, in a way that your queerness isn't. (But even the queerness - it's hard for people who aren't to understand, isn't it?)

==

There is no history. There are no elders, only middle aged weirdos. When you finally make it out to the big city you are warned by the whisper network about which ones will try to fuck you.

Some of your peers go in for that.

==

There is the identity, and then there is the community.

Some of your kind will never associate with the community or go to any gathering, burnt by it. Others disavow you but are are a familiar face at every circuit party regardless.

==

It is a little juvenile, caring about this part of you so much. You're generally expected to outgrow that in a couple of years.

The best of you aren't exactly closeted, but... it no longer consumes them that they are this way, and it's no longer a big part of their identity. They're free to care more about other things. The other things are often also beautiful, and generative, and good.

For whatever reason, you aren't like them.

==

Devon Price writes in a recent post about vampirism and queerness:

Vampires in Rice’s world are afflicted with an all-consuming loneliness —but their only options for companionship are a couple of dozen of other creepy assholes who have interweaving backstories and beef that makes The L Word’s Chart look like a child’s hopscotch drawing. As they fumble through relationships constantly retraumatizing one another, they lack any guidance for how to actually do being a vampire correctly, because all of their elders have already died.

If that doesn’t remind you of your own queer coming-of-age, well, maybe you’re younger and better adjusted than me.

You're too young to have experienced this in the gay community, but the dynamic feels familiar nonetheless.

Price also writes:

As queer people, we are vastly fewer in number than the heterosexual society that surrounds us, and because they have convinced us we are evil and disgusting, we carry a lot of baggage into our every relationship. When we start to find one another, we usually aren’t very good at being loving, but our desperate need to form relationships with one another is also what defines us.

The vampires in Interview have no choice but to find what is lovable in the annoying bitches they have hated for the last three hundred years and the exes who’ve thrown them off of buildings. For us, having a viable social life requires learning to smile across the potluck table at an ex when what we’d really like to do is carve out their throat.

You know, in case you need another reason to not move to the Bay.

==

"Rationalist adjacent". "Post-rat". It's better for you to not be mistaken for one of us, even if you are an ally.

Why shoulder the burden, if you have the option to not?

==

private dm

==

There's no reason that the culture that arose around same-sex attraction would have rainbows and raves and piercings, the concept of camp and haircuts that will make your mom throw up her hands.

There's no reason that the culture that arose around a strange autodidact's warnings about AI progress would have soylent and catgirls and poly, solstice ceremonies and sprawling multi-author fiction written on forum software.

There's no reason. And yet.

==

item.title: AI Safety Acculturation is Neglected
item.description:
At the local AI safety co-working space, there are ~two kinds of regulars.

There's the kind of regular who's been thinking seriously about AI safety and alignment since pre-2022, who have passing to intimate familiarity with the funding ecosystem, the Sequences, and various conferences that happen at Lighthaven. Let's call them rationalists.

Then there's the kind of regular who comes in with many years of impressive industry or government experience, who realized in the last few years that it is important and worthwhile to pivot their career towards making sure that this AI thing is handled competently by the people in power, and who have many valuable skills, insights, and connections that are lacking in rationalist culture. Let's call them professionals.

There are, of course, many people who are somewhere in between - bright undergrads born this millennium who have been involved in EA since stumbling upon 80k hours in high school, professionals who previously identified as EA but drifted out of the scene a few years ago, founders who have idly read some Scott Alexander. But let's call it a dichotomy for now.

There's a large culture gap between the rationalists and the professionals. Robust mutual understanding seems important if we want to work together on this project of not having AI blow up our civilization, and it is only by working together that there is a chance that we might succeed.

Unfortunately, there seems to be an underlying assumption that all you really need to do is stick the two groups in the same room for long enough and the acculturation will happen by default. This seems wrong to me; my experience so far is that there are many unspoken assumptions that are held by the two groups that sort of never come up in conversation, except in weird awkward eruptions when a fundamental assumption is violated. When that happens, the risk is that it pulls the two groups further apart, instead of closer together.

Some examples from recent events and discussions:

  • A recent facilitated discussion where we were encouraged to process our emotions around AI safety, and some people said things like "I feel existential terror at the thought that maybe everyone I love and also our entire species is entirely wiped out in ten years' time" and other people said things like "I am feeling extremely inspired by the amount of driven and intelligent people in the room". I assume that both parties were kind of baffledly thinking "c'mon, dude, read the room" at the other party.
  • A high-effort, small-group serious policy discussion of AI 2040 where most of the room simply could not take the idea of space property rights seriously because it seems like some sort of demented SF libertarian fever dream
  • Me feeling very anxious when I contemplate sharing this piece in the co-working slack, because it's a moderate violation of professional norms that might result in the groups further feeling alienated from each other rather than the opposite

But also, like, timelines, so it seems useful to ask: what might deliberate acculturation look like?

Here are some ideas for how to more deliberately bridge fundamental culture gaps:

  • Beyond speed friending, perhaps a regular AMA/interview type session, where you sit down a singular person in the network for an hour perhaps over lunch, and ask them questions such as: what made you care about AI safety? What's your work/research history like, what's one thing you've done that you're most proud of? What do you think is the most effective lever to change?
  • Encouraging rationalists to hold basic sessions on concepts like "ask vs guess culture", "steelmanning", "double crux"
  • Encouraging professionals to hold basic sessions on concepts like... hmm. This really just doesn't work at all. Rationality has a foundation of explicit, compressible concepts, while professional competence is mostly tacit and procedural, so there really isn't a straightforward analogue. The closest thing might be to get the professionals to share war stories instead, but I think sharing war stories outside of EITHER small groups or up on stage at some several hundred dollar conference is very Not Done in that culture?
  • Maybe I should probably host a session that's just "here are all of the weird idiosyncratic things that rationalists are more likely to believe, ask me questions about them and I won't get mad".
  • God, I really wish there was a professional counterpart to me who can host a session of "here are all of the weird things that professionals are more likely to believe, please ask questions"
  • Establishing common knowledge that acculturation and mutual understanding is a task that needs to be worked on and will not passively happen by default, and people who have a foot in both worlds should consider if it would be useful for them to do something about this

Having written this list out, I am dissatisfied with it because I'm not actually that confident that doing all those things will result in the degree of trust and understanding that I think is necessary for us to do good work together.

What's the actual tension? Perhaps it's that it seems to me like the culturally rationalist are the gatekeepers of the funding resources for work on catastrophic risks, and this feels like a thing that is unsayable and somewhat anti-inductive (in that to explain it is to give an answer key to what funders want to hear, which is not ideal).

Recently a big tent animal welfare conference happened in town and I hosted a mixer for the EAs in attendance (around a third of the ~500-person conference attendees were EA). One of them, a long-established EA, gave me an interesting rundown of the wider animal welfare funding ecosystem. They said that EAs used to not be that accepted in the wider animal welfare movement, but as it became common knowledge that EAs control a large portion of the funding, the community began to embrace them more and adopt more EA frameworks and ways of thinking - but not without some amount of grumbling and resentment and bad feeling in at least some contingents. If you're not EA pilled you will simply resent the fact that the EAs are fundamentally not interested in funding the obviously morally important work of running your local donkey sanctuary, and there's literally nothing you can do about it. And if you are running a local donkey sanctuary you are sort of by definition not EA pilled.

Fortunately for AI safety, the smart policy person who wants to work on compute governance or export controls isn't proposing the AI-safety equivalent of a donkey sanctuary. And unlike the donkey sanctuary owner they have leverage in things rationalists can't buy at any price - things like institutional legibility, standing relationships, tacit knowledge about how to make key organisations do things. And perhaps the problem will also partially solve itself through funder pluralism; the rationalists are not literally the only people on the planet interested in funding alignment research and policy.

Still, I don't want to overstate the case for optimism.

Funder pluralism might result in parallel communities that don't collaborate in the same rooms at all. Animal welfare maybe only avoided this outcome because EA funding was a very significant portion of all funding, but it seems like what the rationalists are gatekeeping is one specific flavour of alignment funding.

Plenty of things professionals consider serious AI work (bias, misinformation, labor displacement, near-term harms) are donkey sanctuaries to at least some parts of the rationalist funding ecosystem, and perhaps it would be useful to make that common knowledge, but that legibility will come at the cost of resentment.

In animal welfare, EAs were newcomers who bought influence into an existing movement. In AI safety, rationalists are more likely to be ~founders, which tilts the balance even more in their favour, which brings with it a deeper (more resentment-building/polarizing) form of gatekeeping.

Bad near-term equilibria that might result (/maybe are already starting to appear) include:

  • The professionals adopt rationalist frameworks because that's where some money is, and quietly grumble, and do not actually fully mean to do what they say they will do in the funding applications
  • The rationalists are required to lossily launder their ideas through professional idiom, and where professional idiom fails them there is no way for them to convey their beliefs in an institutionally legible way

I'm squarely in the rationalist camp, which means that when I see a problem my default response is to write a post and publish it publicly. A skilled professional, on the other hand, would solve problems like these in a way that never produces a public artifact, and because I can't read about how they did it, I can't model what they'd do.

I'm cognizant of the fact that I'm holding only half the puzzle pieces here. If you identify more as a professional than as a rationalist, and reading this post made you feel some type of way, please come find me and give me the other half of the puzzle.

item.title: Notes on Private Trackers
item.description:
In a recentish dialogue, I made a playful sideswipe at the sort of arcane rituals that certain private trackers force prospective inductees to undergo.

The website I was most thinking of + poking fun at is Redacted, a private tracker. They have a standalone website for their study guide here.

Allowing unknowns to get inducted if they pass an interview is a genuine public service. By default, private trackers live up to their names wrt privacy, and the only way to get in is if you can get someone who is already inside to send you an invite. Having a non-nepotism avenue is a ton of additional work, and it's thankless. Actually, it's worse than thankless - it exposes you to many many accusations of gatekeeping and snobbery, which you can avoid entirely by never offering a public avenue at all and disappearing from the public eye.

Once you're in the ecosystem though, then things ease up a lot. A bunch of the private trackers cross-advertise in each others' forums since torrenting etiquette is pretty universal, and if you're good enough for one that's a decent signal that you're good enough for the rest. That being said, there are trackers that are easier to get into and trackers that are more exclusive.

Some people who are pretty into private trackers maintain this wiki page on Reddit, where you can see what's required from you to procure more private tracker invites. If you start at a low prestige tracker and you want to be in a super high prestige tracker, you may need to do up to half a dozen jumps, each of which may take 4-12 months.

The easiest nice private tracker to get invited into is myanonamouse (MAM), which is run by I assume a cabal of housewives; the first, most important rule of MAM isn't about seeding ratios, it's about avoiding swear words. They are so so excited to invite you in and have mods painstakingly walk you through the process of downloading qbittorrent and setting up a vpn. Also they give you credit for seeding as long as you keep the file available, which is very generous. (Most other places count seeding the standard way, which means your upload number only goes up when someone else actually grabs file pieces from you. This can make it difficult to maintain "ratio" - for your uploads to be equivalent or higher than your downloads.) As always, you can always grease the wheels by donating money for server costs.

Friends in other private trackers, including RED, inform me that actually maintaining ratio isn't that hard! I'm not sure why this would be the case, so I don't really believe them.

MAM specializes in ebooks and audiobooks. I don't find their ebook collection to be more impressive than Libgen or Anna's Archive, but their audiobook collection is genuinely top notch. And because of the ratio requirements, each download is incredibly speedy. I've never had a torrent take more than a minute to complete.

Personally, I haven't found a need to join any other private tracker, since I'm not super into old obscure media nor can I hear the difference between 128kbps mp3 and FLAC files.

One interesting recent casualty in this world from the LLMs is bibliotik, which used to be the premier private tracker for books. Then it got scraped and now its name is in a couple of lawsuits levied at the big AI companies, and it hasn't opened up for any new members since.

item.title: Notes on Paying Attention
item.description:
Anything in life can be richer and sweeter if you slow down and pay attention, but some things reward attention more than others.

The different amount of rewardingness per attention is sometimes socially constructed and thus arbitrary to some degree. But it's genuinely nice, to have others who have also paid attention to the thing tell you about the interesting parts that you might have missed, and this can enrich your own experience.

But relying on others to tell you what to pay attention to, and how, is also a bit of a trap. Because each person's umwelt is slightly different from the next, your preferences might legitimately differ from the horde. And only after articulating/distinguishing/understanding your own preferences can you go out into the world and find the other things that will delight you. C.S. Lewis puts it well, in The Problem of Pain:1

You may have noticed that the books you really love are bound together by a secret thread. You know very well what is the common quality that makes you love them, though you cannot put it into words: but most of your friends do not see it at all, and often wonder why, liking this, you should also like that. Again, you have stood before some landscape, which seems to embody what you have been looking for all your life; and then turned to the friend at your side who appears to be seeing what you saw—but at the first words a gulf yawns between you, and you realise that this landscape means something totally different to him, that he is pursuing an alien vision and cares nothing for the ineffable suggestion by which you are transported. Even in your hobbies, has there not always been some secret attraction which the others are curiously ignorant of—something, not to be identified with, but always on the verge of breaking through, the smell of cut wood in the workshop or the clap-clap of water against the boat’s side?

He's right that there's something a little ineffable about it, that secret thread. But you can get to know it better, if you sit with the feeling.

One reason people don't do this is because while paying attention can be rewarding, it could also be risky. After all, what if you are not enjoying something the right way? As Montaigne puts it:

When you have just listened to a whole page of Virgil you can safely exclaim, ‘Now that is beautiful!’ The cunning ones escape that way. But to undertake to go back over the detail of a good author, to try to indicate with precise and selected examples where he surpasses himself and where he flies high by weighing his words and his locutions and his choice of materials one after another: not many try that. [On the art of conversation]

But the ones who want to escape are cowards who are shooting themselves in the foot! You shouldn't be trying to impress other people with your attention. You should be enjoying it for yourself, because paying attention (especially to things you like) is pleasurable. And so you should try to be precise, to give selected examples, and to unapologetically embrace your preferences even when they are embarrassing. And then you should seek out more things that are similar to what you like, to pay closer attention to.

A wonderfully instructive model of paying close attention can be found in Peter Schjeldahl's Hot, Cold, Heavy, Light, a collection of a hundred of his art reviews (he was the New Yorker's art critic from 1998-2022).2 On a Vermeer, for example:

“The Milkmaid”—a diminutive picture, just eighteen inches high by about sixteen wide—is another of the elect, though it’s a mite less absorbing, for me, than the more mature “Young Woman with a Water Pitcher.” Like “Delft,” “The Milkmaid” exercises more dazzling virtuosity than I quite know what to do with. Sensational colors, in particular, strain the scene of a husky young servant pouring milk, in a careful dribble, from an earthenware pitcher into an earthenware bowl on an odd-shaped table laden with a wicker basket, a loaf and fragments of crusty bread, and a stoneware beer jug. (She may be making bread pudding.) She wears a white linen cap, a yellow woollen jacket with green work sleeves, a red skirt, and an apron of a stunningly sumptuous blue.3 The hues jump out from the painting’s miraculous rendering of soft sunlight from a bleared window with a small broken pane that reveals the full brightness of the day. The light spills in a static wave of modulated tones across the dilapidated walls of an apparently rather dank room; the odd stain or nail hole in a wall can grab your eye and not immediately let it go. A boxy foot warmer on the floor calls attention to small baseboard ceramic tiles, one of which, with a blue cartoon of Cupid, may drop a certain hint.

You can notice the same things as Schjeldahl, if you stand in front of The Milkmaid, and stay there for five minutes. He's not exactly making observations that require an art history degree to make!

Closer to home, I'm reminded of Original Seeing from the sequences, and Logan Strohl's naturalism sequence (which aims to communicate what he means by the sentence “knowing the territory takes patient and direct observation"). I think Robert Miles is on a similar wavelength when he divulges his trick for turning foods he dislikes into food he enjoys, and Sasha Chapin when he explains how to like everything more. Probably there are more takes along these lines in woo and meditation communities, but I am allergic to those and have no notes on the matter.

In 2022, I saw Guo Pei's retrospective at the Legion of Honor, which had like eighty of her pieces. Guo Pei is my favourite couture designer — I'm not sure how universal this experience is, but I remember being really excited when I learned about the existence of couture fashion, and then very disappointed when I realized what most collections were like in practice. But Guo Pei, uniquely and delightfully, just keeps delivering on the fantastical experience that I thought couture fashion was at seven years old.

The entire gallery took me thirty minutes or so to finish completely, the first time around. This was a once in a lifetime opportunity (I was in the Bay only for a short time), and I felt disappointed by how little I got out of it. My gaze rested on the intricate dresses, but failed to penetrate, and I knew they would not remain in my memory.

It struck me somehow that more was possible, if only I would pay more attention.

So I decided to do the round again, but this time I was going to play a game with myself. I was going to look at every single one of the intricate outfits on display until each gave me a new idea of how I could dress differently myself. Only then will I move on to the next one. This was an interesting challenge, because in no way can you wear any of Guo Pei's masterpieces on a day to day basis.

my note for this one: try a two-tone outfit but with a gradient element, not just colourblocking.

The acts of seeking and translation slowed me down.

my note for this one: thick ribbons twisted over translucent sleeves of the same colour.

It slowed me down enough, to pay attention.

my note for this one: most of your outfits with vests are dark. experiment with a lighter vest.

I picked up many details that I missed the first time.

my note for this one: two layers is sufficient to create an illusion of many.

The second go-around took long enough that I didn't leave the exhibit until the museum's closing time.

my note for this one: try short bottoms paired with tights and shoes of the same non-black colour.

That experience is the one that taught me to pay attention. What I didn't expect was the joy that I felt, when I slowed down to do it.

Since then, I have tried to pay more attention.





  1. Sadly, this is from a book where he then goes on to proclaim that the reason that you feel this way is because the thing you really yearn for is to go to heaven, a real location.↩

  2. Total tangent: I did not agree the New Yorker is midwit until I read Schjeldahl's collection, and now I kind of think it is. Yes, I think his reviews are a good model of the experience of paying attention to a piece of art, and I would absolutely recommend it to people who are interested in cultivating their own artistic taste. Reading his reviews, you feel permission to look at art for yourself, to not worry about if you're doing it wrong as long as you are actually paying attention - and that is a tremendous gift. So why do I say that it's sort of midwit? Er, deductive reasoning, mostly. I get the overwhelming sense, reading it, that Schjeldahl is performing a level of seeing and understanding that I am now perfectly capable of doing myself. And I know my own taste in art to be supremely midwit :B↩
